title: AI Agents: Turn One Good Workflow Into a Reusable Skill

source.title: Using skills
facts: OpenAI defines a skill as a reusable, shareable workflow for a specific task.
The article describes a skill as a name and description, workflow instructions, and supporting resources.
The article recommends starting from a repeatable task, defining inputs, outputs, and guardrails, then reviewing, installing, and using the skill.
OpenAI notes that skills can be composed as smaller building blocks for complex workflows.

centralThesis: A reusable AI Agent skill is not a longer prompt. It is a tested operating contract that makes the right context, decisions, output format, and checks available at the moment a recurring task begins.
factBoundaries: The source explains general skill workflows, not a guarantee that a skill will solve every task.
The episode's template is a practical interpretation of the source, not an OpenAI product requirement.
reusableArtifact: AI Agent Skill Template: trigger, inputs, workflow, output contract, guardrails, evidence, and revision note.
introTitle: One good result should not become another blank prompt
introPromise: Build a reusable skill that preserves the useful workflow without pretending every task is identical.
summaryTitle: The reusable skill is a working contract
summaryPromise: Capture the repeatable judgment, attach the right resources, and improve the contract from evidence.
hookPain: People repeatedly reconstruct prompts, constraints, and output formats after a good AI-assisted result.
hookGap: The viewer needs to see how a skill turns a successful run into an inspectable workflow without freezing the wrong assumptions.
rejectedHook: Do you want AI Agents to be more useful?

chapters.title: Find the repeat
chapters.body: Start with a task that keeps returning, not with a document you hope people will read.

recaps.narration: A skill begins with a recurring job, not a generic topic.
The trigger should make clear when the workflow applies.
One-off exploration can remain a conversation.

chapters.title: Keep the useful context
chapters.body: A skill should fetch the context that changes the decision, not every detail from the last project.

recaps.narration: Inputs explain what the Agent can use.
Constraints explain what it must protect.
References belong beside the step that needs them.

chapters.title: Write the decisions
chapters.body: The heart of a skill is a small sequence of decisions that a capable teammate could inspect and challenge.

recaps.narration: Separate the goal from the method.
Write branches only where a real choice exists.
Ask for evidence when a judgment is high risk.

chapters.title: Define the handoff
chapters.body: A reusable workflow ends with an output another person or Agent can check, edit, and continue.

recaps.narration: Specify the format before execution starts.
Make unknowns visible instead of hiding them.
Include a final check that matches the task.

chapters.title: Improve by evidence
chapters.body: Treat a skill as a maintained asset: revise it after failure patterns, not after every passing mood.

recaps.narration: Record the failure that justified a revision.
Keep small skills composable rather than creating one giant prompt.
Retest the workflow on a fresh task.

segments.text: Why does an AI Agent repeat your best work instead of building on it? The answer is not a longer prompt. It is a reusable skill that carries the parts of the workflow worth repeating.
segments.screenText: Turn a good workflow into a reusable skill

segments.text: OpenAI describes skills as reusable, shareable workflows for specific tasks. A skill can carry a name, instructions, and supporting resources so the next run starts from a useful operating pattern rather than a blank chat.

The loss is familiar: you finally get a good research brief, handoff, analysis, or draft, then reconstruct the same context, constraints, and formatting rules next week. The result is inconsistency before the real work even begins.

In this video, you will build an AI Agent Skill Template with seven fields: trigger, inputs, workflow, output contract, guardrails, evidence, and revision note. It is small enough to use and explicit enough to inspect.
segments.screenText: The seven-field AI Agent Skill Template

segments.text: Before we begin, save the idea that a useful skill does not replace judgment. It removes the avoidable setup work so your judgment can focus on the parts that are genuinely new.
segments.screenText: Reuse the setup, not your judgment

segments.text: Look for a repeat that has a recognizable starting signal. For example, a weekly customer summary starts when fresh notes and product data arrive. The skill should describe that trigger, not merely say that it creates summaries.

A repeatable task has stable intent, even when the source material changes. If the goal, audience, and success condition are different every time, you still have exploration, not a workflow ready to package.

Do not mistake frequent copying for repeatability. A copied prompt may contain a useful sentence, but a skill earns its place when the same decisions, checks, and deliverable shape recur across several real runs.
segments.screenText: Copying is not yet a skill

segments.text: Write the trigger in ordinary language: when a decision-ready update is needed from new evidence, use this skill. That sentence prevents a good workflow from being activated for a nearby but different job.
Next, list the inputs that change the answer. A source folder, a customer brief, a target audience, a deadline, and an approved vocabulary can matter. Old decorative examples usually do not.

Resources work best when they sit beside the step that needs them. A research workflow can point to the source standard during evidence collection and to the delivery template only when the final brief is assembled.

Make constraints concrete. Instead of saying be careful, specify what must not be invented, which records are authoritative, which action requires approval, and how uncertainty should be shown to the reviewer.
This is also where a skill differs from memory. Memory can remember a preference or prior fact. A skill tells the Agent which context to retrieve, how to use it, and what to do when it conflicts.
segments.screenText: Memory stores; a skill directs work

segments.text: Now write the workflow as a short sequence of decisions. Begin with the goal, inspect the inputs, identify missing information, choose a method, create the draft, and verify the promised outcome.
Each step needs a reason to exist. If a step only repeats what the previous step already required, remove it. If a step changes the evidence, the choice, or the handoff, make that change visible.
segments.screenText: Every step should change the state

segments.text: Use branches sparingly. A useful branch sounds like this: if the source is incomplete, ask for the missing record and label the draft as provisional. It does not try to predict every imaginable exception.
For high-risk claims, demand an evidence move. The Agent can cite the record, show a calculation, name an assumption, or ask a human to decide. A confident sentence alone is not a verification step.

A good skill ends with a handoff contract. Define the audience, format, required fields, and the decision the output should support. This lets a reviewer check the result without reverse-engineering the original prompt.

Include an uncertainty rule. If a source is missing, if two records disagree, or if a decision depends on human preference, the output should surface that condition instead of burying it in fluent language.

The final check should match the task. A release note needs factual and link checks. A customer message needs audience and permission checks. A plan needs owners, next steps, and unresolved decisions.
segments.screenText: Match the check to the work

segments.text: This makes skills shareable. Another teammate does not need your private intuition to judge whether the run succeeded. They can inspect the input, the decisions, the output contract, and the evidence.

Do not freeze a skill after its first success. Record the failure pattern that led to a revision: a missing input, a misleading default, a weak output field, or a check that looked reassuring but missed the real error.
Keep the unit small. One skill can gather evidence, another can turn evidence into a decision brief, and a third can run a release check. Smaller skills are easier to understand, test, and recombine.

Retest after a revision on fresh work. Replaying the exact example that inspired the skill proves only that you preserved the past. A new input reveals whether the instructions carry the right judgment forward.

When a skill becomes too long, ask which part is truly shared and which part belongs in a resource, a template, or a separate specialized skill. The goal is reliable guidance, not a monument to every past lesson.

The practical sequence is simple. Capture a real repeat, name the trigger, bring in the context that changes decisions, write the few steps that matter, define the handoff, and test the result against a fresh case.

That is how an AI Agent stops replaying your best prompt and starts using a maintained working method. The skill does not make the Agent infallible. It makes the work easier to inspect, improve, and reuse.
segments.screenText: A skill turns success into a method

segments.text: Try the template on one small recurring task this week. Write the trigger in one sentence, attach only the source material that changes a decision, name one check a reviewer can actually perform, and record one uncertainty that the Agent must not smooth over. If that version helps a second real run, keep it. If it fails, revise the field that failed instead of adding unrelated instructions everywhere.
segments.screenText: Start small, then revise from evidence

metadata.description:
AI Agent skills help you turn a successful workflow into a repeatable method without flattening the judgment that still needs a human.
Use the seven-field template to define the trigger, context, decisions, output, checks, and revision evidence.

What you'll learn:
- How to identify work that is actually repeatable
- How to write an AI Agent skill as an inspectable decision path
- How to test and improve a reusable workflow
